title: There Will Always Be More Excuses Than Reasons to Act
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: The author argues that the standard advice to "stop making excuses" fails because most excuses are true: you really are tired, the timing really is bad, and the thing might really fail. Shaming a true statement does not make it false, and the debate itself becomes the delay. His reframe is that an excuse is a true fact with a conclusion borrowed onto it ("I am tired, so not today"), and the fact never actually dictates the conclusion. He draws on Epictetus, who separated an impediment to the leg from an impediment to the will, and on Cleanthes, who arrived in Athens with four drachmas and worked nights watering gardens so he could study under Zeno. The piece is honest that some obstacles, such as illness or caregiving, require a different route or help rather than more force. The practical method is to write the reason as a full sentence, agree with it without a "but", and then do the smallest thing still possible today. Because it targets self-discipline and follow-through, it sits with the archive's leadership and character material.
points: Most excuses are true statements, so shaming or arguing against them fails; the useful question is what to do while they are still standing there.
An excuse is a fact plus a decision that has borrowed the fact's authority, and separating the two removes the excuse's power over action.
Epictetus and Cleanthes show that obstacles change the method, not the aim: Cleanthes took notes on oyster shells and watered gardens at night.
The author concedes that real obstacles sometimes call for a different route or outside help rather than more force on the same plan.
The method is concrete: state the reason in a full sentence, agree with it with no "but", then name the smallest step a tired person can still take today.
